newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croat refugees visit graves in Serb enclave.
newsitem.headline: Croat refugees visit graves in Serb enclave.

text.p: Croatian refugees from Eastern Slavonia made their first visit in years to the Serb-held enclave on Friday to commemorate their dead on All Saints Day and catch a glimpse of their homes.
Their visit, unthinkable only 12 months ago, results from a deal between the presidents of Serbia and Croatia on the fringes of the Dayton peace talks last November.

Eastern Slavonia, together with two other enclaves in Croatia, was seized by minority Serbs in mid-1991 when they rebelled against Zagreb's drive for independence from former Yugoslavia and expelled thousands of non-Serbs from the region.
The area was put under U.N. Transitional Administration (UNTAES) control in January after the Croatian army recaptured the other Serb enclaves. It should revert to Croatian rule sometime in 1997.
Some 40 buses carrying more than 2,000 refugees crossed over to Serb-held territory on Friday morning escorted by UNTAES, the U.N. civil police, and joint Croat-Serb police patrols.
Men and women, some dressed in black and carrying flowers, were allowed a one-hour visit to 30 grave sites scattered all over Eastern Slavonia, where UNTAES said it could guarantee their safety.
For some of the refugees the visit symbolically marked the start of a long delayed return to their homes in the rich farmland.
"This is the beginning of our return...Next time we'll go back for good," said 62-year-old refugee Vladimir Cacic before boarding a bus near the Croatian town of Osijek.
The visit, carried out under tight security, passed without incident, as both local police and the U.N. prevented contact between Croatian refugees and the enclave's Serb residents.
An UNTAES spokesman confirmed to Reuters all refugees left the region safely after the visit. But others said extra precautionary measures had been taken.
"We didn't drive through Vukovar. We used backroads, although many refugees expressed the wish just to see the town again," captain David Lanier of the U.N. civil police in the town told Reuters.
"It's just that there are still some people in town who are not quite ready for this kind of normalisation," he said.
Some 250 Croats visited the city cemetery in Vukovar, a town reduced to rubble by Serb rebels and Yugoslav army guns in 1991.
The U.N. tried to strip the event of political significance and journalists and local Serbs were banned from the grave site during the visit.
Fresh flowers and wreaths, laid at dozens of graves marked with austere wooden crosses at the far end of the cemetery, were the only evidence of the visit.
"It was really emotional, quite a scene, when the refugees came to the graves for the first time in five years... But everybody was very polite on both sides," Lanier said.
"I haven't been to my village for so long," said Zuzana Romer, 52, whose mother is buried at one of the cemeteries. "I am going there to see my home too, and so are most of the people."
"I was shocked to see how dirty and messy everything has become after we left," a woman told local Osijek radio upon return. "But now I know we'll go back soon".
